item.title: Kasama Pottery Workshop: 250 Years of Ceramic Tradition — Guide
item.description: Kasama-yaki, the pottery of Kasama, is one of Japan’s leading ceramic traditions, with a history stretching back roughly 250 years and prized for its simple, functional beauty rather than ornate decoration. The town is home to several hundred kilns and studios, many open to visitors for hands-on workshops where beginners can try wheel-throwing (rokuro) or freehand painting on pre-fired pieces, taking home a piece they made themselves after a firing and shipping period.

item.title: Nikko Woodcarving Workshop: Try the Craft Behind the Shrine's Carvings — Guide
item.description: Nikko’s tradition of fine woodcarving developed directly from the small army of skilled carpenters and carvers assembled to build Toshogu shrine in the early 1600s, whose techniques were passed down through generations and remain the foundation of the region’s celebrated craftsmanship, visible in the shrine’s famous carvings including the three wise monkeys. Several studios around Nikko now offer hands-on workshops where visitors can learn basic carving techniques under the guidance of trained artisans, working on a small wooden piece to take home.

item.title: Takaoka Copperware: A Hands-On Metalworking Craft Experience — Guide
item.description: Takaoka has produced copperware and bronze casting for over 400 years, a tradition dating back to the early Edo period when the local feudal lord invited metalworking craftsmen to the area, and the industry remains active today, producing everything from temple bells to fine decorative objects. Visitors can try hands-on workshops in the city’s craft district, working under the guidance of local artisans to shape, polish or finish their own small copperware piece to take home as a souvenir of the experience.

item.title: Takasaki Daruma: Japan's Daruma Doll Capital — Guide
item.description: Takasaki produces roughly 80% of all daruma dolls made in Japan, a craft tradition dating back over 200 years to a local temple priest who taught the technique to farmers as a winter income source. The round, hollow, red-and-white papier-mâché figures — purchased with blank eyes to set a wish or goal, with one eye painted in upon purchase and the second added once the goal is achieved — are produced at dozens of workshops around the city, some open for hands-on painting experiences, and each January the city hosts one of Japan’s largest daruma markets at Shorinzan Darumaji temple.

item.title: Aizu Lacquerware Painting Workshop: A 400-Year Craft Tradition — Guide
item.description: Aizu-nuri lacquerware is one of Japan’s foremost lacquerware traditions, dating back over 400 years to when a feudal lord invited lacquer artisans to Aizu to develop the local craft as an economic industry. The result is a distinctive style known for its warm gold and vermillion maki-e decoration, and today, workshops throughout Aizu-Wakamatsu let visitors try their hand at painting a small lacquerware piece — such as a bowl, chopsticks or small box — under the guidance of trained artisans, taking home a genuinely handmade souvenir.

item.title: Miyagi Tansu: Iron-Fitted Traditional Cabinetry — Guide
item.description: Miyagi tansu are traditional wooden chests renowned across Japan for their lustrous zelkova (keyaki) wood grain and elaborate hand-forged iron fittings, crafted using techniques passed down since the Edo period. Each piece can take months to complete, with the wood aged and polished to a deep reddish sheen and the iron hardware hand-hammered into intricate patterns — a genuine heirloom-quality craft still practised by a small number of Sendai-area workshops.

item.title: Omiya Bonsai Village: The Spiritual Home of Japanese Bonsai — Guide
item.description: Omiya Bonsai Village was founded in the 1920s when a group of Tokyo bonsai growers relocated here after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, seeking clean water and open land suited to cultivation. Today the neighbourhood remains the recognised spiritual home of Japanese bonsai, with several working nurseries open to visitors displaying trees, some centuries old, alongside the Omiya Bonsai Art Museum, the world’s first public museum dedicated entirely to the art form.

item.title: Kakunodate Kabazaiku: 200-Year Cherry Bark Craft — Guide
item.description: Kakunodate’s 200-year-old craft tradition of kabazaiku uses cherry tree bark to create lustrous, durable containers, tea canisters and accessories. The bark is peeled, layered and polished to a warm honey-brown sheen — a uniquely Akita art form born from the samurai district’s need for a secondary income. Several workshops in the samurai quarter welcome visitors to watch artisans at work. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kakunodate, Senboku, Akita Hours Workshops ~9:00–17:00 Admission Free to browse; pieces vary Time needed 45 min–1.
